title: Anchors and word boundaries
explanation:
Without anchors, a pattern matches **anywhere** in the string: `/cat/` finds "cat" inside "bobcat". **Anchors** pin the match to a position without consuming characters:

- `^` matches the beginning of the input and `$` the end. Use both to require that the *whole* string fits the pattern: `/^\d+$/` accepts `"2026"` but not `"2026a"`.
- With the `m` (multiline) flag, `^` and `$` also match right after and right before line breaks, so they work line by line.
- `\b` is a **word boundary**: a position between a word character and a non-word character (or the string edge). `/\bon\b/` finds the word "on" but not the "on" in "noon". `\B` is the opposite — a position that is *not* a boundary.

```js
console.log(/^\d+$/.test("2026"), /^\d+$/.test("2026a"));   // true false
console.log(/^b$/m.test("a\nb\nc"));                         // true: m makes ^ and $ per line
console.log("on noon".match(/\bon\b/g));                     // [ 'on' ]
```

Anchors and boundaries are **zero-width**: they test a position and match no characters, so they never appear in the matched text.
keyIdeas: `^...$` requires the whole input to match; add `m` to work per line.
`\b` sits between a word character and a non-word character.
Anchors are zero-width: they match positions, not characters.

workedExample.problem: In `"redo the prereq, then reread"`, find every word that **starts with** `re`.
steps: `re` alone would also hit the middle of "prereq" — we need the match to begin at the start of a word.
Put a word boundary in front: `\bre`. No boundary at the end, because the word continues.
Consume the rest of the word with `\w*`, and add the `g` flag to collect all matches.
workedExample.answer: `["redo", "reread"]` with `/\bre\w*/g`; without `\b` the pattern also returns `"rereq"` from inside "prereq".

pitfalls: Forgetting `^` and `$` in validation, so `"abc123xyz"` passes a digits-only check.
Expecting `^`/`$` to match at every line without the `m` flag.
Relying on `\b` with accented letters: `\w` is ASCII-only, so `é` counts as a non-word character.

citations.quote: Input boundary beginning assertion: Matches the beginning of input. If the multiline (m) flag is enabled, also matches immediately after a line break character.
Input boundary end assertion: Matches the end of input. If the multiline (m) flag is enabled, also matches immediately before a line break character.
This is the position where a word character is not followed or preceded by another word-character, such as between a letter and a space.
Some of the remaining metacharacters to be discussed are zero-width assertions. They don't cause the engine to advance through the string; instead, they consume no characters at all
Matches any alphanumeric character from the basic Latin alphabet, including the underscore.
